html:
A qanat is an underground channel that carries groundwater by gravity from beneath the hills to fields and towns lower down, a technique developed in ancient Iran about three thousand years ago. It let farming and cities thrive on the dry Iranian plateau, where rivers are few and rain is scarce.

Builders found water under a hillside and dug a mother well down to it. From there they cut a gently sloping tunnel out to the surface, sometimes for many kilometres. Vertical shafts every few dozen metres let them remove earth and get air. From the air, a qanat looks like a line of craters across the desert.

Its advantages:

  • No pumps or animals were needed; the water flowed by itself, day and night.
  • Underground, the water hardly evaporated in the desert heat.
  • It tapped water steadily, without draining the aquifer as modern pumps do.

Qanats fed the oasis towns of Iran, such as Yazd, and the walled Persian gardens, images of paradise in a dry land. Water rights were shared among villagers by strict schedules.

The idea spread widely. Under the Achaemenid Persians qanats were dug in Egypt's Kharga Oasis. After the Arab conquests they spread across North Africa, where they are called foggara and khettara, and into Spain. They are called karez in Afghanistan and in Turpan in western China. Along with the windmills of Iran, they show how people in dry lands learned to work with very little water. Many still run, but deep pumped wells are drying up a lot of them.
